children: By Jan Wolfe
Democratic US lawmakers, emboldened by decisive victories in this month's
, have vowed to pursue sweeping investigations of US President
and his administration once they take control of Congress in January.
But the

's 6-3 conservative majority has embraced a robust vision of executive authority and expanded the power of the presidency. The court also has issued rulings in recent years that could impede congressional investigations. Here is a look at how the court and its rulings could come into play.
WHAT IS THE ADMINISTRATION PLANNING?

Some Democratic lawmakers have promised to pass out subpoenas "like candy" or "Mardi Gras beads," with Senator Ed Markey saying, "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing."
Trump's White House and Justice Department are signaling their intention to resist congressional probes.

White House counsel Will Scharf wrote a letter last week to Robert Garcia, incoming chairman of the House of Representatives Oversight Committee, saying the administration is "monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators." Scharf said inquiries by lawmakers targeting the ‌administration could themselves be considered criminal and worthy of Justice Department investigation.

Congressional investigations focused on Trump also may be hamstrung by two Supreme Court decisions involving his conduct during his first term as president — one in 2020 involving a congressional subpoena to his accounting firm, and one in 2024 recognizing broad presidential immunity from prosecution for actions taken in office.
DOES CONGRESS HAVE LEGAL AUTHORITY TO INVESTIGATE THE EXECUTIVE BRANCH?
Yes, but with limits. Congress has been conducting oversight of federal agencies since 1792, when the House created a special committee to investigate a US military loss to Native American forces.

The Supreme Court made clear in a 1927 ruling that either chamber of Congress has the implied constitutional authority to conduct investigations, including inquiries into the executive branch, and compel testimony in order to carry out its legislative duties. In that case, a Senate committee was investigating the Justice Department's failure to prosecute people involved in the Teapot Dome scandal, a corruption affair during President Warren Harding's administration.

That and other Supreme Court precedents make clear that, once Democrats take control of congressional committees on January 3, they can issue legally binding letters known as subpoenas that compel a person or organization to produce documents or testify under oath.

The Supreme Court in various cases has made clear that Congress must be able to investigate the scope of a problem in order to propose legislative solutions, stating in the 1927 decision that "the power of inquiry — with process to enforce it — is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function."
While the court has affirmed the broad investigative power of Congress, it has also said lawmakers cannot inquire into purely private affairs unrelated to potential legislation.
WHAT HAPPENS IF THE ADMINISTRATION DEFIES SUBPOENAS?
Congress passed a law in 1857 that makes willfully defying a valid congressional subpoena, called contempt of Congress, a misdemeanor criminal offense, punishable by up to a year in prison.
Such prosecutions are rare, but the Justice Department has brought a handful in US history after receiving a referral from congressional leaders.

Two Trump advisers, Peter Navarro and Steve Bannon, were convicted of contempt of Congress after refusing to cooperate with a Democratic-led congressional committee that investigated the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by Trump supporters who tried to prevent lawmakers from certifying the results of the 2020 election he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.

Navarro and Bannon were the first people found guilty of contempt of Congress since the 1974 conviction of G. Gordon Liddy, a conspirator in the Watergate scandal that led to President Richard Nixon's resignation.

Navarro last month asked the Supreme Court to throw out his conviction, saying he had a good-faith belief that a legal doctrine called executive privilege prevented him from complying with the subpoena. That request is pending.
Trump's Justice Department is considered unlikely to prosecute his advisers for contempt of Congress.

The Supreme Court stated in an 1821 decision that Congress has the inherent authority to direct a security officer, known as the sergeant at arms, to arrest and detain recalcitrant witnesses. The last time Congress exercised this authority, known as "inherent contempt," was in 1934, and the practice is seen as unlikely to make a comeback.
A more common tactic is for congressional leaders to authorize a civil lawsuit that seeks a court order requiring compliance with a subpoena.

The Justice Department, under presidents of both parties, has argued that the courts lack jurisdiction to hear disputes between Congress and the executive branch over testimony. The Supreme Court has never definitively ruled on the matter.
ARE THERE LIMITS ON INVESTIGATING A PRESIDENT?
The Supreme Court in recent years has raised constitutional concerns about congressional investigations targeting a sitting president, though the law in this area is not fully settled.

In the landmark 2020 ruling in a case called Trump v. Mazars USA LLP, the court addressed a subpoena issued by a Democratic-led House committee to Trump's longtime accounting firm that sought his personal financial records covering an eight-year period.

In its 7-2 decision, the court said that, when Congress subpoenas a president's financial records, a general assertion of a legislative purpose is not enough. The court sent the matter back to a trial judge who had previously upheld the subpoena, explaining that a subpoena should not unduly burden the president and that the lawmakers needed to better explain how their request was as specific as reasonably possible.
The committee in 2022, after Trump left office, reached a settlement with the accounting firm that allowed the lawmakers to access a narrower set of documents than they had initially sought.
The landmark 2024 Supreme Court decision in a case called Trump v. United States also could undermine congressional investigations into the president.

The court decided that a president cannot be prosecuted for actions that fall under the constitutional powers of the office. The decision also stated that Congress should not intrude on core executive powers, like the president's pardon power or authority to fire officials.
"Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the president's actions on subjects within his 'conclusive and preclusive' constitutional authority," the ruling stated.
By limiting the authority of Congress to legislate in certain areas, that decision also may have weakened the ability of lawmakers to conduct legislative oversight over the executive branch.
CAN A PRESIDENT KEEP CONVERSATIONS WITH ADVISERS PRIVATE?

Yes, the Supreme Court said in a 1974 decision involving President Richard Nixon that executive privilege allows the president and top executive branch officials to keep certain internal communications confidential and to resist subpoenas.

Executive privilege is based on the idea that a president needs to be able to have candid, private discussions without the immediate fear of public scrutiny or political interference. The privilege cannot be used to cover up wrongdoing, the Supreme Court ruled in the Nixon decision.

Trump's Justice Department in August issued a memo asserting that executive privilege can extend to private advisers and individuals outside the executive branch. That legal theory has not yet been tested in court.
